progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C11 and Year 11: a dissolved ionic compound is separate hydrated ions and dissolving depends on more than one factor (C11); ionic formulas from ion charges, polyatomic ions (nitrate, sulfate, carbonate, hydroxide, ammonium), balancing equations, state symbols and meeting precipitation reactions in Module 3 (Year 11). Not assumed: Ksp, Qsp, solubility rules.
progression.startsWith: Two clear colourless solutions, potassium iodide and lead nitrate, giving a bright yellow solid, with the question of where the solid came from and what is left in the liquid.
progression.stopsAfter: Listing the ions in two solutions; swapping partners and checking both products against supplied or learned rules; naming the precipitate (and its colour for the three syllabus pairs); writing the molecular, full ionic and net ionic equations with spectators identified and charge checked; recognising no precipitate with no net ionic equation; stating which ions remain dissolved after filtering, including an excess reagent. No Ksp, no Qsp, no water-treatment selectivity, no conduct of the investigation.
progression.nextLesson: P03: investigating the solubility rules yourself (practical support); then C14: Ksp, putting a number on insoluble.

teaching.task: Predict what forms when two ionic solutions are mixed, write the molecular, full ionic and net ionic equations, and say what stays dissolved.
teaching.causalExplanation: Each bottle holds separate hydrated ions, so mixing gives four kinds of ion and the only new thing possible is new partners. One new pair holds together in a solid more than it stays hydrated, so it comes out as a precipitate, and the other ions stay dissolved and unchanged as spectators. The solubility rules summarise which pairs do this and were found by experiment, so both products are checked because either could be the insoluble one. The solid is not dissolved ions, so it is never split in the ionic equation, and the spectators are identical on both sides, so they cancel to leave the net ionic equation. Charges must balance, which is why lead iodide has two iodides. After filtering, the solution holds the spectators plus any ion that was added in excess, because it has no partner left.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Starts from a yellow solid appearing from two clear solutions, shows the four ions and the new partners, gives the cause of a precipitate and the spectators, summarises the rules in order, then works the three syllabus pairs one equation line at a time with a charge check, adds the no-precipitate case and the filtrate, gives two memory aids and asks two unseen items with a short pause and brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Two clear solutions make a bright yellow solid, and neither bottle had anything yellow in it. Where did the solid come from, and what is left in the liquid?
teaching.understandingCheck: Copper(II) sulfate and sodium hydroxide are mixed: name the precipitate and write the net ionic equation. Then silver nitrate is mixed with more than enough sodium chloride and the white solid is filtered off: which ions are in the filtrate?
teaching.curriculumScope: Predict and analyse the composition of substances when two ionic solutions are mixed, for example potassium chloride and silver nitrate, potassium iodide and lead nitrate, and sodium sulfate and barium nitrate (Module 5, ACSCH065). The video predicts and analyses and does not replace the investigation. Ksp, Qsp and water-treatment selection are deferred.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, the painted lead iodide tube pair, painted reagent bottles with coded labels, the painted precipitate tubes, the painted barium meal glass, coded hydrated-ion lenses, a coded rules card, swap cross and three-line equation stack with flying ion tokens and strikes, and an abstract filter funnel. Colour key: positive ions amber, negative ions violet, water shells pale blue, the precipitate always in its real colour, spectators grey when struck.
design.transitionPlan: The bottles and the tube open the lesson and the bottles stay in the left column; the two lenses merge into one over the tube; the grid becomes the rules card and the card shrinks to the corner for the swap cross; the equation stack adds one line per scene and clears between pairs; the filter funnel carries the filtrate scene and attempt 2; the attempt boards clear the aids and the feedback rebuilds the cross, the stack or the lens; the next chips slide in; scene crossfade with settle.

Where did the solid come from?" writes on; on "what's left" a pen ring circles the liquid above the solid with a "?" tag
